newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-TRAPATTONI UTTERS THE UNTHINKABLE AT BAYERN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-TRAPATTONI UTTERS THE UNTHINKABLE AT BAYERN.

text.p: Bayern Munich's experienced Italian coach Giovanni Trapattoni has uttered the unthinkable as his team prepare for their city derby with 1860 Munich on Friday -- scrapping the cherished libero position.

Trapattoni is keen to introduce a back four at Bayern to replace Germany's traditional 3-5-2 system with two man-to-man markers and a libero -- the tactics which took Germany to this year's Euro 96 triumph in England.

On the surface it may look like an uninteresting tactical change from the former AC Milan and Juventus supremo but in Bavaria it is about as popular as a Munich mayor announcing that he is banning beer, sausages and sauerkraut.

It was at Bayern that World Cup-winning coach and player Franz Beckenbauer turned the libero role into a key ingredient of footballing tactics in the 1960s and 1970s. Germany has been looking for a player to match his skills ever since.
Understandably, Beckenbauer, now Bayern chairman, prefers the old system -- as do many of Bayern's players.
"You have an extra man in the middle and that is where the goal is," the 1990 World Cup-winning coach said simply.
Germany captain and striker Juergen Klinsmann added: "A 3-5-2 or 5-3-2 system suits our players better."
Trapattoni, however, has said he wants to experiment.

Friday's return of German international defender Thomas Helmer from injury has given the coach extra scope although it is doubtful that he will take the plunge in Helmer's first game. Changes at the back are likely to come soon, however.
While it may not be AC Milan v Inter Milan or Liverpool v Everton, the Munich derby has a great deal of history attached to it.
When Beckenbauer first joined Bayern in the 1960s, 1860 were Munich's biggest side and Bayern were not even in the first division when it was started in 1963.
Inspired by the likes of Beckenbauer, Gerd Mueller and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Bayern have since won a record 13 titles while 1860 went down to the regional league in Bavaria.
Now, after bouncing back to the top flight in the 1990s, 1860 have held their own in the first division and are presently ninth in the Bundesliga.

The atmosphere will be intense in Munich's Olympic stadium as second-placed Bayern look to take over the top of the table. But Bayern captain Lothar Matthaeus is playing down the significance of the match.

"We have to sort out the championship -- not 1860," Matthaeus said. "Every match is important. But they have gone from an amateur club to UEFA Cup candidates. Everyone has respect for this superb achievement."

Only goal difference separates Bayern from leaders VfB Stuttgart who travel to struggling St. Pauli on Saturday. Reigning champions Borussia Dortmund, who are fourth, are also involved in a local derby at Schalke on Saturday.
